t: Maximum Profitable Triplets With Increasing Prices II — Fenwick Trees for Prefix Max
o: Same problem as the Medium version but with n up to 50000, so O(n^2) is too slow. Prices are conveniently bounded by 5000, letting us index Fenwick trees directly by price. For each middle item j we need max profit among earlier items with price < prices[j] and later items with price > prices[j]; both are dynamic prefix/suffix-maximum queries answered by BITs in O(log(maxPrice)).
k: Fixing the middle element splits the problem into a left prefix-max and a right suffix-max query over price.
Because prices ≤ 5000, we can use price itself as the BIT index — no coordinate compression needed; a reversed-index trick turns suffix-max into prefix-max.

a.n: Approach 1: Two Fenwick trees (forward and backward passes)
a.i: Scan left to right: before inserting item j, query the BIT for the maximum profit among inserted items with price < prices[j] — that is left[j]. Scan right to left symmetrically with a BIT indexed by (MAXP+1-price) so 'price greater than p' becomes a prefix query. Combine.
s: Build left[]: for j = 0..n-1, left[j] = BIT1.query(prices[j]-1), then BIT1.update(prices[j], profits[j]).
Build right[]: for j = n-1..0, right[j] = BIT2.query(MAXP - prices[j]), then BIT2.update(MAXP+1-prices[j], profits[j]).
Answer = max over j with both sides nonzero of left[j]+profits[j]+right[j], else -1.
a.t: O(n log MAXP) — two BIT passes with log(5000) per operation
a.sp: O(MAXP) — two Fenwick arrays of size 5001

w: This is essentially the only viable complexity class for the Hard constraints; a segment tree over compressed prices works identically if prices were unbounded. Pitfalls: off-by-one on the strict inequalities (query price-1 and MAXP-price respectively), and reusing one BIT for both directions. Follow-up: generalize to k-tuples, or to online insertion with deletions.
